intro: How New Zealand taxes income from managed funds and KiwiSaver funds that are portfolio investment entities, which rates apply, and what happens if the wrong one is used.
explanation:
## What a PIE is

Savings held in a managed fund of the kind called a portfolio investment entity (PIE) are taxed under special rules. A person's KiwiSaver scheme might be such a fund. In a multi-rate PIE, tax on an investor's income is worked out at a rate that belongs to that investor.

## The three rates

The rate is called the prescribed investor rate (PIR). A New Zealand resident individual has three to choose from, shown on this page. They cannot choose 0%. Which one fits depends on how much the person earned over the past 2 tax years, and Inland Revenue (IRD) provides a set of questions that works it out. The two years counted are the two tax years before the current one.

A person with a temporary tax exemption lasting 4 years may use a 0% rate, but only by investing in a zero-rate PIE.

## Giving the PIE your rate

An investor gives the PIE their rate and their IRD number when the account is opened, and has to tell the PIE if the rate changes. Each year a PIE will ask its investors to check that their rate is still right. Someone investing for the first time gets 6 weeks to pass on an IRD number. After that the PIE may close the account and return the money, minus tax.

If no rate is given, the PIE uses the highest rate, which is also the default.

## If the wrong rate was used

At the end of the year, IRD works out what the tax should have been, using the correct rate. Too much tax paid produces a PIE credit, which is offset against any income tax owing, and any remainder is refunded. Too little produces a PIE debt, which is added to the person's income tax bill. A higher rate used when a fund makes a loss can also leave the investor with a debt, because the loss credit given was larger than the one they were entitled to.

## Other effects

A locked-in fund, a KiwiSaver scheme for example, keeps its PIE income out of the Working for Families and student loan calculations. Income from a fund without that lock, or a payout from a listed PIE, does go into them, and myIR lets the person adjust the figure. Someone who withdraws a whole investment during a quarter, from a PIE that files quarterly and calculates tax at the zero rate, may owe tax at the end of the year.
